From Proto-Finnic *uhkëda. Cognate to Finnish uhkea and Votic uhka.
From Proto-Finnic *huima. Cognate with Finnish huima and Ingrian huima.

From Proto-Finnic *vajëh. Cognate to Finnish vaihe and Votic vahõ.

From võlu + -r, from Proto-Finnic *vëlho.

parole.significato: about, amount, by, much (used to indicate inexact quantities in comparison to something else)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Finnic *vërta, from Proto-Germanic *werþaz. Cognate with Finnish verta.
From Proto-Finnic *vërkko. Cognate with Finnish verkko.
From Proto-Finnic *vësa. Cognate to Finnish vesa and Livonian võzā.

parole.significato: key (a tool to open and close a lock)
parole.testo: From Proto-Finnic *vot'in, equivalent to võtma (“to take”) + -i. Cognates include Votic võtti (“key”), Livonian võțīm (“key”) and Finnish otin (“handle”).

parole.significato: to take (to get into one's hands, possession or control, with or without force)
parole.testo: From Proto-Finnic *vottadak, possibly from Proto-Uralic *watta-. From Proto-Finnic *veeras. Cognates include Finnish vieras and Votic võõrõz. Possibly from same root as in veer; or a Baltic loan, compare Lithuanian vyras.
From Proto-Finnic *vöö.
From Proto-Finnic *äkedä. Cognate to Finnish äkeä and Votic äččü. See also äkki.

parole.significato: to wheeze, to grunt (to breathe heavily, usually after physical activity)
parole.testo: From Proto-Finnic *ähkidäk, ultimately onomatopoetic. Cognate with Finnish ähkiä and Ingrian ähkää.

From Proto-Finnic *äijä (“old man”), from Proto-Finno-Permic *äjjä (“old man”). Cognates include Finnish äijä (“old man”), Votic äjje, Ingrian äijä (“grandfather; father-in-law; old man”), Karelian äijä (“a lot of”), Livvi äijy (“many, much”), Ludian äij (“a lot of”), Veps äi (“many, much”); Norther
From Proto-Finnic *äges.
From Proto-Finnic *äkkidä. Cognate to Finnish äkkiä and Votic äčči. Possibly the same root as in äge.
From Proto-Finnic [Term?]. Cognate with Finnish hämähäkki and Votic hämö.
From Proto-Finnic *ämmä. Cognate with Finnish ämmä and Votic ämme.
From Proto-Finnic *erä. Related to eri.

parole.significato: to awaken (to cause to become awake)
parole.testo: From Proto-Finnic *heräit'äk. By surface analysis, ärkama + -tama.

From Proto-Finnic *ääri. Cognate with Finnish ääri.
From Proto-Finnic *hëhku.

parole.significato: evening (the end of the day, usually from about six o'clock until bedtime)
parole.testo: From Proto-Finnic *ëktago. Cognate with Finnish ehtoo and Votic ohtogo.
Derived from Proto-Finnic *ohut, probably from Proto-Uralic *wokše. Cognate with Finnish ohut.
From Proto-Finnic *oikëda. Cognate with Finnish oikea, Veps oiged, Võro õigõ.

From Proto-Finnic *häici, borrowed from Proto-Baltic [Term?]. Compare Lithuanian žiedas and Latvian zieds. Cognate with Finnish hede, hedelmä, Veps heiditä (“to blossom”), and Votic edʹdʹittsä (“to blossom (mainly used for rye)”).
From Proto-Finnic *olka.
From Proto-Finnic *olki.

From Proto-Finnic *ombëldak. Cognate to Finnish ommella and Votic õmmõllõ. Compare also Inari Sami uubbalm (“needle”).
From Proto-Finnic *onni.
From Proto-Finnic *onnët'oin, equivalent to õnn + -tu. Compare Finnish onneton.
From Proto-Finnic *op'ëttadak, from the same root as õppima.
From Proto-Finnic *oppidak. Cognate with Finnish oppia.
From Proto-Finnic *horna. Cognate to Livonian vōrna (“tender”), Karelian hornie (“cool, lukewarm”), and dialectal Finnish horna, hornea (“cool, lukewarm”).

parole.significato: horror, terror, dread (feeling of profound fear)
parole.testo: From Proto-Finnic *outo. Cognate with Finnish outo (“strange, weird”), Karelian outo.

From Proto-Finnic *öö, from Proto-Finno-Ugric *üje. Cognates include Ingrian öö, Ludian üö, Finnish yö, Karelian yö, Livonian īe, Northern Sami idja, Inari Sami ijjâ, Erzya ве (ve), Udmurt уй (uj), Komi-Permyak ой (oj), Komi-Zyrian вой (voj), Southern Mansi йӣ (jī) and Hungarian éj.

parole.significato: to barf, retch, keck, vomit, throw up
parole.testo: From Proto-Finnic *öökkidäk. Compare Votic ööčütellä (“hiccup, burp”) (Mati), Finnish yökätä, Livvi yökkiä. Cognates might also include Eastern Mari ӱгынчаш (ügynčaš, “hiccup”), Udmurt вукпотыны (vukpotyny, “nauseate, make someone puke”), Komi-Zyrian вӧк (vök, “disgust, nastiness”, noun) and Hungari

From Proto-Finnic *üdin, from Proto-Finno-Ugric *wideme. Cognate with Finnish ydin (“core, kernel; marrow”), Karelian yjin, Livvi üdin, Northern Sami ađa (“(bone with) marrow”) (from Proto-Samic *ëδëm), Erzya удем (udem, “brain, intellect; marrow”), Eastern Mari вем (vem, “brain; marrow”), Udmurt ви
From Proto-Finnic *ükteksä.
From Proto-Finnic *ükteksänci.

From Proto-Finnic *ükteksä toicta kümmentä. Equivalent to üheksa (“nine”) + teist (“of second”). Shortened from üheksateistkümmend ("nine of the second decade"), which is still evident in declension. Cognate with Finnish yhdeksäntoista.
From Proto-Finnic *ükci, from Proto-Finno-Ugric *ükte. Cognates include Finnish yksi.

From Proto-Finnic *ükci toicta kümmentä. Equivalent to üks (“one”) + teist (“of second”). Shortened from üksteistkümmend ("one of the second decade"), which is still evident in declension. Cognate with Finnish yksitoista.
From Proto-Finnic *ülpedä, most likely derived from üle (“over”). Cognates include Finnish ylpeä, Votic and Ingrian ülpiä and Livvi ylbei.
From Proto-Finnic *üli.

parole.significato: to serve, to be a servant
parole.testo: From Proto-Finnic *ümbärtädäk. Cognate to Finnish ymmärtää.

parole.significato: to say (to verbally express information, opinion, attitude, feelings, etc. in words)
parole.testo: From Proto-Finnic *jut'ëldak, by surface analysis, jutt + -lema, with an irregular change ju > ü in the first syllable. The form jütlema (“to preach”) can be found in some older texts.

parole.significato: a year (a solar year, the time it takes the Earth to complete one revolution of the Sun: between 365.24 and 365.26 days…
parole.testo: From Proto-Finnic *aigasta-aika, from *aigasta (“from time”), and *aika (“time”), possibly borrowed from either Proto-Germanic *aiwaz (“long time, eternity”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂óyu ~ *h₂yéws (“long time, lifetime”), from *h₂ey- (“vital force, age”), or from earlier *ajeka and borrowed from
From Proto-Finnic *halmëh. Cognate to Finnish halme and Livvi halmeh. From either Proto-Germanic *halmaz or a Baltic language, compare Latvian salms and Lithuanian želmuo.

parole.significato: Refers to a hypothetical or hoped-for possibility that is not entirely certain: perhaps, maybe
parole.testo: From Proto-Finnic *ehkä, cognate with Finnish ehkä, Votic ehči, Karelian ehki. Possibly derived from the negative verb stem *e-, whence modern Estonian ei, or from an identical Proto-Uralic stem meaning 'this', from which et. From Proto-Finnic *hëlma, borrowed from either Baltic (cf. Lithuanian šelmuo (“ridge (of a roof)”)) or Proto-Germanic *helmaz (“protective covering”). Cognate with Finnish helma.

From Proto-Finnic *kaja. Alternatively, and less likely, a deverbal from kajama (“to echo”), from Proto-Finnic *kajadak. From Proto-Finnic *kauka-, either from Proto-Germanic *hauhaz, or from Proto-Finno-Ugric *kawka, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kewk-. Compare Erzya кувака (kuvaka, “long, lengthy”) and Northern Khanty ҳөв (ḥøw, “faraway, long”). Cognate to Finnish kauko- and Votic kauga.
From Proto-Finnic *laito, possibly from Proto-Baltic *slaid-. Compare Lithuanian šlaitas (“hillside”). Cognate to Finnish laito. Alternatively from Proto-Germanic *laidō.

parole.significato: to find (to discover something intentionally or by accident)
parole.testo: From Proto-Finnic *leütädäk, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *hleutaną. Alternatively from the same root as lööma.
From Proto-Finnic *mëtu, from either Proto-Germanic *meduz or Proto-Balto-Slavic *medú. Cognate to Votic mõtu (“mead, beer”) and dialectal Finnish metu (“nectar, honey, juice”).

From Proto-Finnic *müüdäk, *möödäk, from Proto-Uralic *mixe- (“to give”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂mey-gw-. Cognate with Finnish myydä, Veps möda, Võro müümä. From Proto-Finnic *napa, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃nebʰ- (“navel”) either through Germanic or Baltic.

parole.significato: wake (a party held in the honour of the dead, after a funeral)
parole.testo: From Proto-Finnic *peijeh, probably from Proto-Indo-Iranian *paiyas, or alternatively from Proto-Germanic *faigijaz. Compare Old Norse feigr (“near death”) and Sanskrit वाजपेय (vāja-péya, “ritual drink when sacrificing, potion of strength”). Cognate with Finnish peijaiset, peijaat, and Karelian peij

parole.significato: piglet (a young pig that is not yet middle-aged)
parole.testo: From Proto-Finnic *porcas, from Proto-Finno-Permic *porćas, ultimately from Proto-Iranian *párćas or possibly Proto-Indo-European *pórḱos (compare Ancient Greek πόρκος (pórkos), Latin porcus, Northern Kurdish purs and Lithuanian paršas). Cognates include Finnish porsas, Livonian pūoraz, Votic põrzõz

From Proto-Finnic *rugis, borrowed from either a Baltic or Germanic language, compare Lithuanian rugys and Proto-Germanic *rugiz. Cognate with Finnish ruis, Votic rüiz, ruiz, Veps rugiž, and Livvi ruiš.
Derived from Proto-Finnic *rehkidäk, probably borrowed from Proto-Germanic *þreskaną, or alternatively of onomatopoeic origin. Compare Finnish rehkiä.

From Proto-Finnic *cüvä (compare Finnish syvä), possibly from Proto-Finno-Ugric *tiwä (compare e.g. Livonian tõvā, Northern Sami davvi (“north”), Eastern Mari тӱнӧ (tünö)) or from Proto-Germanic *deupaz (“deep”).

parole.significato: to know (to have information, knowledge about something, to be aware of something)
parole.testo: From Proto-Finnic *teetädäk, probably derived from Proto-Finnic *tee (“road, way”) (modern Estonian tee). In this case the verb seems to have originally meant ’to know the way’. Cognates include Võro tiidmä, Livonian tied, Votic täätä; Finnish tietää, Ingrian tiitää, Livvi tiediä, Ludian tieta, Veps

From Proto-Finnic *vaino, borrowed from Old East Slavic воина (voina, “war”). Compare Russian война (vojna, “war”). Cognate with Finnish vaino. Alternatively of Baltic origin; compare Latvian vaina (“fault, guilt”). The word appears in older literature often with the meaning of "war".

Most likely from Proto-Finnic *ouvi, from Proto-Uralic *owe. Compare Finnish ovi and Votic õvvi. Alternatively, and less likely, possibly a Low German loan, as in hoov, in which case the Votic word would be a loan from Estonian.
